Apple last month filed a lawsuit against OpenAI, accusing the company behind ChatGPT of stealing trade secrets related to hardware development. Nearly a month later, OpenAI has responded in detail to Apple's multiple allegations in a blog post.

First, here's a brief timeline as background:

  • July 10: Apple sues OpenAI, alleging that former Apple employees systematically stole Apple's trade secrets to benefit OpenAI's future hardware business.
  • July 10: OpenAI issues a brief statement in response: "We have no interest in any other company's trade secrets. We will continue to focus on building innovative technologies that empower users worldwide."
  • July 14: OpenAI updates its response, saying it has yet to see any evidence supporting Apple's allegations.

Then on August 4, OpenAI published a blog post that evening, finally responding in greater detail. You can read the full article here.

The article is titled "Apple got it wrong" and published under OpenAI's byline.

OpenAI's latest response first characterises the lawsuit as "reckless, aggressive, and unusually targeting individuals":

OpenAI then appears to suggest that they were not properly notified about the relevant matters before being formally sued, including some details that have already been reported before today:

They subsequently provided relevant email correspondence records, which can be viewed on the webpage.

The response then finally acknowledged some of the data access issues raised by Apple:

If you have read Apple's original complaint, you will know that Tang Tan is one of the key figures in the complaint. OpenAI's latest response defends Tan:

The remainder of the response contains only two paragraphs of text, after which it switches to screenshots of emails and iMessages. Below is the concluding statement:

We wish Apple had communicated with us about these issues before formally filing the lawsuit, and we would be happy to explain all relevant circumstances to them. We have taken the allegations in the complaint seriously and expressed our willingness to work with Apple to resolve the matter. However, Apple has instead attempted to shift the direction of its narrative, including making vague accusations against other former employees, and is likely to continue using this approach. Apple's application for a temporary injunction is both based on misinformation and entirely unnecessary, because we neither have nor want any of their trade secrets. What interests us more is building innovative products and technologies that push the boundaries.

That is roughly the current situation. This is not a formal legal response, but in the three and a half weeks since Apple filed the lawsuit, this is the most OpenAI has said (and shown).

Just a reminder, you can read OpenAI's latest response here, and learn about Apple's original complaint here.
